Technical note · October 2026 · Belu Sochim

ipau: a System-One judge beside the robot policy

A 23M-parameter model that answers typed questions about a robot's situation, is this subtask done, which phase are we in, how far along is this step, in 7 ms, from camera frames, with calibrated probabilities and no text generation. It replaces the simulator's ground truth inside a π₀.₅ control loop and matches a fine-tuned 7B vision-language model on a public process-understanding benchmark.

7ms
per decision, two camera views, RTX 6000 Ada. π₀.₅ takes ~100 ms per action chunk on the same GPU.
23M
parameters total: a frozen 22M vision encoder plus 0.7M of trained heads. No decoder.
30/ 51
task successes with the judge in the loop, vs 25/51 with ground truth and 16/51 with nothing.
42%
phase-recognition accuracy on RoboProcessBench, vs 44% for a 7B VLM fine-tuned on the same split.

Why a robot needs a judge

Vision-language-action policies generate motion. They do not generate judgments. In our runs, π₀.₅ fine-tuned on a two-step kitchen task put the cookies in the basket on every attempt and then failed the second step two times out of three: it re-grasped the cookies or froze, because nothing told it the first step was over. The information that would fix this is a yes/no answer, available every control step, which is exactly the shape of decision that TypeSafe's Jev made fast and cheap for software by refusing to generate text. ipau is that primitive for robots.

Architecture

Results

1. In the loop: the judge replaces the simulator's ground truth

Same π₀.₅ checkpoint, same 51 new seeds, one variable: who says a subtask is done. The policy runs on the training primitives ("pick cookies", "place cookies into basket", …) and the prompt advances when the judge fires.

Who decides "subtask done"Task success95% CISubtask completionWon / lost vs fixed, by seed
Nobody: one fixed task prompt16 / 51 · 31%20–4566%—
The simulator's ground-truth stage checks (oracle)25 / 51 · 49%36–6274%—
ipau, the 7 ms judge30 / 51 · 59%45–7179%21 / 7

Across the 51 episodes the judge fired on 50 of 51 first-stage completions and 30 of 31 second-stage completions, a median 44 and 28 environment steps after the true event, with zero early or false fires and one miss. The delay is the persistence rule: it waits for five confident samples at one sample per ten steps. The judge-versus-oracle difference is inside the confidence interval; the honest claim is that it matches ground truth.

2. Benchmark: process questions, same split as the released baseline

RoboProcessBench asks multiple-choice questions about robot manipulation clips. We train on the GM-100 training rows and score the 2,643 evaluation rows, exactly the protocol of the authors' fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B, whose released predictions we rescore on the same subset. Zero-shot Claude models run through the benchmark's own prompt template. Model selection uses a validation split of training episodes; the evaluation set is scored once.

3. Does the policy already know? No.

If π₀.₅'s own vision-language representation carried these answers, a probe on it would make the judge free. We extracted π₀.₅'s prefix features, the same pass its action expert reads, for every frame above and trained the same heads on them.

The policy's representation knows when the cookies are in the basket and barely knows when the sauce is, which is the stage it fails. A VLA's encoding is shaped for predicting the next action, not for judging the scene. A separate judge with its own encoder is the right design, and it is cheap enough that there is no reason not to have one.

4. Where it came from: memory needs a judge

Method

Training data and labels

  • Stage completion. 204 recorded episodes of π₀.₅ on the task, 39k frames sampled every 10 steps, labelled by the benchmark's own stage checks: free, and on the policy's visual distribution including its failures. Demonstrations from the dataset did not transfer for the second stage: demonstrators move differently from the policy.
  • Benchmark questions. The 12,857 GM-100 training rows; question and option text embedded with bge-small; the scorer sees ordered frame features, a question-attended frame context, and the first-to-last change across the clip.
  • Calibration. Thresholds and persistence are chosen on held-out episodes at a fixed early-fire budget, the conformal recipe used by SAFE and FIPER. Confidence is the concentration of the output distribution, as in Jev.

Limitations

  • One task and one checkpoint in the loop; 51 episodes per arm. The judge-versus-oracle gap is noise; the judge-versus-nothing gap is not.
  • Within-episode stage detection is the judge's job here; which prompting strategy a task needs was learned by the memory layer in an earlier experiment and fixed for this one.
  • Frozen generic features. Motion direction and bimanual coordination need spatial-temporal detail that pooled features lose; the fine-tuned 7B model is far ahead there.
  • One benchmark source of four. The other three require datasets we have not obtained.
  • No calibration-aware training yet. The heads are trained with cross-entropy; Jev's reported trick, rewarding honest probabilities, is the next step.

What is next

  • The action-chunk chooser: the policy samples N chunks, the judge scores them in one batched pass. Prior work gains 8 to 25 points this way but at 650 ms; at 20 ms it can run every step.
  • Read the policy's features where they help (contact) and keep the separate encoder where they do not (progress).
  • Multi-task over the benchmark's 26 tasks and transfer across policies.

Reproduce

git clone https://github.com/Phillips-Ugo/memory_robotics && cd memory_robotics
uv run python -m jev.frames --every 10 --features dinov2_vits14          # stage labels + features from recordings
uv run python -m jev.train_head --features dinov2_vits14,dinov2_vits14_wrist --window 3
uv run python -m jev.rpb build && uv run python -m jev.rpb train           # RoboProcessBench, GM-100 split
bash scripts/x6_pod.sh                                                     # the in-the-loop run (one GPU)

Raw results for every table above are committed under docs/results/, and the research log records each run with dates, seeds and costs.

Jev is TypeSafe AI's model; this work borrows its framing and is not affiliated. π₀.₅ is Physical Intelligence's policy, used through openpi. RoboProcessBench and RoboMemArena are their authors' benchmarks.
